static.title: Seeing a planet beside its star
static.note: Two different problems stand between a telescope and a planet. The planet must be far enough from its star on the sky (an angle), and it must be bright enough against the star’s glare (a flux ratio, the contrast). The diffraction scale λ/D belongs to the telescope; a coronagraph’s inner working angle is a separate number that belongs to the instrument. The four instruments here are teaching examples: their working angles and contrast floors are not the specifications of any real instrument.

samples.label: Planet
samples.value: Earth around the Sun: seen from 10 parsecs at a phase angle of 90 degrees; orbit 1.0 AU, star 5772 K

samples.label: Separation
samples.value: 0.1000 arcseconds on the sky: 1.000 AU, which is the orbit’s radius times the sine of the phase angle

samples.label: Diffraction scale
samples.value: λ/D is 0.0189 arcseconds for 6.0 m at 0.55 micrometres, and the separation is 5.3 λ/D. λ/D is the telescope’s diffraction scale. It is not a coronagraph’s inner working angle.

samples.label: Inner working angle
samples.value: 3 λ/D, which is 0.0567 arcseconds: a teaching value for this example, not a cited specification of any instrument

samples.label: Contrast
samples.value: reflected 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰, thermal 1.5 × 10⁻⁴⁷, total 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰: the planet is 8.5 × 10⁹ times fainter than its star at 0.55 micrometres

samples.label: Can this instrument see it?
samples.value: Outside the inner working angle and brighter than the contrast floor of 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰: this example instrument could see it. The panel does not model the starlight suppression, so this is a necessary condition and not a prediction.

samples.label: Temperature
samples.value: The planet is drawn as a blackbody at 254 K, what starlight alone gives it (a Bond albedo of 0.31).

samples.label: Assumes
samples.value: Blackbody planet and star; a Lambert sphere with the stated geometric albedo; a circular orbit; the separation is the orbit’s radius times the sine of the phase angle; the contrast is a flux ratio of the unresolved bodies; no starlight suppression, speckle noise or exposure time. Where the plot drops below 10⁻¹⁶ it is drawn at that value.

static.title: Ver un planeta junto a su estrella
static.note: Dos problemas distintos separan a un telescopio de un planeta. El planeta debe estar lo bastante lejos de su estrella en el cielo (un ángulo) y debe ser lo bastante brillante frente al resplandor de la estrella (un cociente de flujos, el contraste). La escala de difracción λ/D es del telescopio; el ángulo de trabajo interno de un coronógrafo es otro número, propio del instrumento. Los cuatro instrumentos de aquí son ejemplos didácticos: sus ángulos de trabajo y sus pisos de contraste no son las especificaciones de ningún instrumento real.
